And the Edessenes were relieved from the heavy taxes.
Then Nasr descended upon the Persians, the faction of Tahir;
and by fifties and by hundreds they seized them and slaughtered them like sheep.
And Nasr and Amr, the rebels, went up against Edessa to plunder it,
and they waged a fierce battle against it.
And the Persians, along with the citizens, went up onto the wall and fought,
while even the women carried stones up for the fight,
and water for the drink of the fighters.
And those who were not able to go up
were kneeling in prayer,
"among whom I was one,"
says Patriarch Mor Dionysius of Tell-Mahre.
And the Lord had mercy,
and Amr was swallowed up,
and the rebels departed.
When the people of Baghdad saw the power of the rebels,
and that al-Ma'mun was far away, they brought al-Ma'mun's uncle,
namely Ibrahim son of al-Mahdi,
and made him king.
Then Hasan, the general of al-Ma'mun,
who had fled to Aqula from the disturbance,
prepared for battle with the people of Baghdad.
And Tahir, who was in Callinicus, appeased the rebels:
some of them with gifts,
and some of them he put in power over territories.
He appointed Ibrahim the Qurayshite over Harran.
While he was walking around in his high dome-chamber in Harran,
he saw new buildings.
And when he asked the Arabs around him,
they said to him:
"They are churches of the Christians, which they built in your days,
and on account of this the Muslims are offended with you."
Then he became enraged and ordered the destruction of the new churches.
And before the sun set, they destroyed the altar of our Great Church which was in Harran,
and that of the Mother of God which was in Quba,
and a little of the temple of Mor George,
and other temples belonging to the Chalcedonians, Nestorians, and Jews.
And that very night, as he slept,
God terrified him in a dream;
and in the morning he summoned the Christians and said
that they should rebuild whatever had been destroyed.
And in a few days they built back all that had been ruined.
And that Ibrahim permitted the Harranian pagans to perform their mysteries openly.
They reached such boldness
that they adorned a bull with costly garments, crowned it with flowers,
hung little bells on its horns,
and led it around in all the streets with songs and flutes.
And thus they offered it for the sacrifice of their gods.
And he appointed Abd al-Ala over Edessa.
And he was very harsh on them with tributes.
